blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Motivation theories are broadly split into Content Theories (focusing on what motivates) and Process Theories (focusing on how motivation works).
Leadership theories explore different approaches and styles of guiding teams effectively.
Organisational culture defines the shared values, norms, and atmosphere within an enterprise.
Group dynamics and team management involve understanding interactions and collaborative efficiency.

cells: 5 levels: Physiological → Safety → Social → Esteem → Self-Actualisation; lower needs must be satisfied before higher ones become motivators
Bank employees at lower levels need job security, fair wages; senior employees need recognition and growth opportunities
Condenses Maslow into 3: Existence, Relatedness, Growth; frustration-regression: if higher need frustrated, person regresses to lower; multiple needs simultaneously
More realistic than Maslow; allows simultaneous needs; explains why senior employees still focus on pay (existence)
Hygiene Factors (prevent dissatisfaction :salary, job security, company policy) vs Motivators (create satisfaction :achievement, recognition, growth, responsibility)
Distinguish between hygiene (minimum required) and motivators (drive performance); bank HR must go beyond just good pay
3 needs: nAch (Achievement), nAff (Affiliation), nPow (Power); high nAch prefers challenging tasks with moderate risk
Bank managers high in nAch suited for sales/business development; high nAff for customer service; high nPow for leadership

blocks.content: Process Theories of Motivation (How motivation works)

cells: Motivation = Valence × Instrumentality × Expectancy; Valence = value of outcome; Instrumentality = performance leads to reward; Expectancy = effort leads to performance
Employees compare their input/output ratio with referent others; perceived inequity (over/under-reward) motivates behaviour change; basis of pay equity grievances
Specific, challenging goals with feedback improve performance; SMART goals; goal commitment; participative goal-setting most effective
Behaviour shaped by consequences: positive reinforcement, negative reinforcement, punishment, extinction; variable ratio reinforcement most powerful
Intrinsic vs extrinsic motivation; basic psychological needs: autonomy, competence, relatedness; over-reliance on extrinsic rewards undermines intrinsic motivation
Leaders born with certain traits: intelligence, dominance, self-confidence, energy, initiative, integrity
Identify traits for leadership selection; limited as situation also matters; early approach
Blake and Mouton's Managerial Grid (1964): concern for task vs concern for people; 9×9 grid; Team Leader (9,9) is ideal
Leadership style training; assess orientation; develop balanced leaders
McGregor (1960): Theory X = employees lazy, avoid work, need control; Theory Y = employees self-motivated, responsible, seek challenge
HR policies and management philosophy; participative management; Theory Y alignment
Hersey and Blanchard (1977): leadership style depends on follower's readiness/maturity; 4 styles: Telling, Selling, Participating, Delegating
Match leadership style to employee development level; flexibility crucial
Robert House (1971): leader's role to clarify path to goals; 4 styles: Directive, Supportive, Participative, Achievement-Oriented
Reduce obstacles; provide guidance; increase rewards for goal achievement
Exchange-based; contingent reward; management by exception; short-term focus; leader-follower transaction
Day-to-day management; performance management; incentive systems in banks
Inspire and motivate; 4 I's: Idealised Influence, Inspirational Motivation, Intellectual Stimulation, Individualised Consideration (Bass & Avolio)
Drive cultural change in banks; post-merger integration; innovation; empowerment
Greenleaf (1970): leader serves followers first; builds others; humility; listening; stewardship
Post-crisis banking reform; ethical banking; ESG leadership

items: Memory Check: Ensure you can differentiate Content Theories ('What motivates') from Process Theories ('How motivation works').
Expect questions linking Leadership Theories and Group Dynamics to real-world organisational scenarios.

cells: Shared values, beliefs, norms, and assumptions that shape behaviour in an organisation; 'the way things are done here'; Edgar Schein's model
1. Artefacts (visible :buildings, dress, rituals); 2. Espoused Values (stated values, strategies); 3. Basic Underlying Assumptions (unconscious, taken-for-granted beliefs)
Widely shared; deeply held; guides behaviour consistently; high alignment; e.g., SBI's 'Banker to Every Indian' culture
Diverse subcultures; low alignment; more individual discretion; typical in fast-growing organisations
Power Distance; Individualism/Collectivism; Masculinity/Femininity; Uncertainty Avoidance; Long-Term Orientation; Indulgence vs Restraint
Leadership modelling; communication; training; reward systems; hiring for cultural fit; long-term process; resistance expected
M&A often fails due to cultural incompatibility; need cultural due diligence; integration plan; communication; post-merger HR role
Forming (orientation, getting to know) → Storming (conflict, struggle for roles) → Norming (cohesion, standards) → Performing (productive, collaborative) → Adjourning (dissolution, reflection)
Created by organisation; specific task or function; permanent or temporary; work teams, project teams, committees
Naturally formed; based on common interests, friendships, proximity; powerful in shaping culture; grapevine is informal communication channel
Degree to which members are attracted to and motivated to remain in group; high cohesion + aligned goals = high performance; high cohesion + misaligned goals = low performance
Janis (1972): excessive consensus; suppress dissent; poor decisions; symptoms: illusion of invulnerability, rationalisation, self-censorship; prevent with devil's advocate, diverse teams
Individuals exert less effort in groups than alone (Ringelmann Effect); address with individual accountability, smaller teams, peer evaluation
9 roles: Plant (creative), Resource Investigator, Coordinator, Shaper, Monitor Evaluator, Teamworker, Implementer, Completer Finisher, Specialist; balanced team needs different roles
